Let’s talk about Chapter 6: Embedding Hybrid and Remote Practices into Organizational Culture.
Now that your team’s got the basics down, the real challenge is making these new ways of working feel totally natural—like they’ve always been part of who you are as an organization.
Think of your company culture as the soil where everything else grows. If it’s healthy—filled with trust, openness, and adaptability—well, just about any new idea can take root and thrive. But if the soil’s dry or neglected, even the best tools and plans might struggle to survive.
Here’s something important: in a hybrid or remote setup, culture doesn’t just happen on its own. It takes real intention. Leaders need to be clear about what they value, show those values in action, and keep reinforcing the right habits.
That might mean updating your mission or values so they actually fit the realities of remote work. Or, it could look like creating new team rituals that help everyone feel connected—even when you’re all miles apart.
Picture this: some companies kick off each new hire with a virtual welcome ceremony, bringing the whole team together online to say hello. Others hold regular “show and tell” sessions, where folks share recent wins or lessons learned. These simple rituals do wonders for building community—even when you can’t all be in the same room.
Another powerful tool? Storytelling. When people share stories—about overcoming tough challenges, finding creative solutions, or pulling together as a team—it brings your values to life. Leaders can encourage this by inviting team members to share their experiences in meetings, newsletters, or even on internal forums.
So, what are some practical ways to weave hybrid and remote practices into your culture?
First, there’s values-based hiring and onboarding—making sure you’re bringing on people who really get—and support—your approach to distributed work.
Then, there’s visible leadership modeling, where leaders walk the talk and consistently show the behaviors they want everyone else to follow.
And finally, cultural rituals: regular events or routines that keep people connected, learning, and united by a shared purpose.
Let’s look at a real example. Imagine a global design firm that holds monthly “culture calls.” Employees from every region join in to share updates, celebrate milestones, and talk through challenges. Over time, these calls turn into a kind of anchor—helping everyone feel part of something bigger than just their immediate team.
Remember, embedding new practices into your culture isn’t a one-and-done project. It’s a journey. You’ll need patience, persistence, and the flexibility to adapt as your organization grows and changes. But when you get it right, you create a solid foundation—one that supports high performance, no matter where your people are working.
